claim: The dorsal (DCIC) and lateral cortices (LCIC) of the inferior colliculus are major targets of the auditory and non-auditory cortical areas.
source: The dorsal (DCIC) and lateral cortices (LCIC) of the inferior colliculus are major targets of the auditory and non-auditory cortical areas, suggesting a role in complex multimodal information processing.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established anatomical knowledge about IC connectivity.

claim: Both GABAergic and non-GABAergic neurons in the mouse dorsal IC showed spatial microheterogeneity in their temporal responses.
source: Both GABAergic and non-GABAergic neurons showed spatial microheterogeneity in their temporal responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing different response classes across spatial locations.

claim: A robust, double rostromedial-caudolateral gradient of frequency tuning was conserved between GABAergic and non-GABAergic neurons.
source: In contrast, a robust, double rostromedial-caudolateral gradient of frequency tuning was conserved between the two groups, and even among the subclasses.
evidence: This is supported by the tonotopic mapping data shown in Figure 6 and related analyses.

claim: A subset of neurons in the dorsal IC is sensitive to spontaneous movements.
source: This, together with the existence of a subset of neurons sensitive to spontaneous movements, provides functional evidence for redefining the border between DCIC and LCIC.
evidence: This is supported by the movement-related activity data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The inferior colliculus is usually divided into three main regions: the central nucleus (CNIC), the lateral cortex (LCIC), and the dorsal cortex (DCIC).
source: The IC is usually divided into three main regions: the central nucleus (CNIC), the lateral cortex (LCIC), and the dorsal cortex (DCIC; Oliver, 2005).
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The DCIC and LCIC are part of the non-lemniscal pathway.
source: The latter two, together also known as the 'shell region' of the IC, are part of the non-lemniscal pathway, and are heavily innervated by feedback projections from the cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about IC organization.

claim: The DCIC and LCIC are heavily innervated by feedback projections from the cerebral cortex.
source: The latter two, together also known as the 'shell region' of the IC, are part of the non-lemniscal pathway, and are heavily innervated by feedback projections from the cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about IC connectivity.

claim: The LCIC is characterized by distinct neurochemical modules visualized with acetylcholinesterase or NADPH diaphorase staining.
source: The LCIC is characterized by distinct neurochemical modules, which can be visualized with various histochemical methods such as acetylcholinesterase or NADPH diaphorase staining, as well as dense labeling of GABAergic terminals and sparse calretinin immunoreactivity (Lesicko et al., 2016; Dillingham et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The LCIC modules show dense labeling of GABAergic terminals and sparse calretinin immunoreactivity.
source: The LCIC is characterized by distinct neurochemical modules, which can be visualized with various histochemical methods such as acetylcholinesterase or NADPH diaphorase staining, as well as dense labeling of GABAergic terminals and sparse calretinin immunoreactivity (Lesicko et al., 2016; Dillingham et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LCIC modules show a distinct complement of Eph-ephrin guidance molecules during development.
source: These modules show a distinct complement of Eph-ephrin guidance molecules during development (Wallace et al., 2016; Gay et al., 2018) and receive input from non-auditory areas (Lesicko et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2017), hinting at their integral role in multisensory integration in the IC.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous developmental studies.

claim: LCIC modules receive input from non-auditory areas.
source: These modules show a distinct complement of Eph-ephrin guidance molecules during development (Wallace et al., 2016; Gay et al., 2018) and receive input from non-auditory areas (Lesicko et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2017), hinting at their integral role in multisensory integration in the IC.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The DCIC and LCIC are at the surface of the mouse brain, making the dorsal IC accessible for in vivo imaging.
source: The DCIC and LCIC are at the surface of the mouse brain, making the dorsal IC an accessible structure for in vivo imaging (Geis and Borst, 2013; Barnstedt et al., 2015; Babola et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous imaging studies and anatomical knowledge.

claim: Around one-fourth of neurons in the IC are GABAergic.
source: Around one-fourth of neurons in the IC are GABAergic (Schofield and Beebe, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Large GABAergic neurons in the IC form a distinct subclass.
source: In particular the large GABAergic neurons seem to form a distinct subclass (Ito et al., 2009; Ito and Oliver, 2012; Geis and Borst, 2013), but based on histology, at least four different subclasses of GABAergic neurons can be discriminated, which all contribute to the ascending projections to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus (Beebe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At least four different subclasses of GABAergic neurons can be discriminated in the IC based on histology.
source: In particular the large GABAergic neurons seem to form a distinct subclass (Ito et al., 2009; Ito and Oliver, 2012; Geis and Borst, 2013), but based on histology, at least four different subclasses of GABAergic neurons can be discriminated, which all contribute to the ascending projections to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus (Beebe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: All four subclasses of GABAergic neurons in the IC contribute to ascending projections to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus.
source: In particular the large GABAergic neurons seem to form a distinct subclass (Ito et al., 2009; Ito and Oliver, 2012; Geis and Borst, 2013), but based on histology, at least four different subclasses of GABAergic neurons can be discriminated, which all contribute to the ascending projections to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus (Beebe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The large majority (95%) of GCaMP-positive neurons in the GP4.3 line were not positive for GAD67.
source: The large majority (4651/4898; 95%) of GCaMP-positive neurons in the GP4.3 line were not positive for GAD67 (Figure 1A–D), showing that the Thy1-promoter preferentially expressed GCaMP6s in non-GABAergic cells in the IC.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Thy1-promoter in GP4.3 mice preferentially expressed GCaMP6s in non-GABAergic cells in the IC.
source: The large majority (4651/4898; 95%) of GCaMP-positive neurons in the GP4.3 line were not positive for GAD67 (Figure 1A–D), showing that the Thy1-promoter preferentially expressed GCaMP6s in non-GABAergic cells in the IC.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunohistochemistry data showing that 95% of GCaMP+ cells were GAD67-negative.

claim: Not all non-GABAergic cells in the IC were GCaMP-positive in GP4.3 mice.
source: Not all non-GABAergic cells were GCaMP-positive, as shown by the NeuN-positive, GCaMP-negative cell bodies in Figure 1C (arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GCaMP6s-positive neurons in GP4.3 mice are enriched at the border of neurochemical modules characterized by dense GAD67 terminals.
source: In particular, we observed that GCaMP6s-positive neurons are enriched at the border of neurochemical modules characterized by dense GAD67 terminals (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: More than 93% (1702/1828) of GCaMP-positive neurons in Gad2;Ai96 mice expressed GAD67.
source: In contrast, we detected GAD67 immunoreactivity in >93% (1702/1828) of GCaMP-positive neurons in the Gad2;Ai96 mice (Figure 1D,H–O).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Not all GAD67-positive cells in Gad2;Ai96 mice were labeled by GCaMP6s.
source: Not all GAD67-positive cells in this mouse line were labeled by GCaMP6s (e.g. arrowheads in Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: A large majority (94%) of GCaMP+ cells in GP4.3 did not show strong immunoreactivity for parvalbumin or calretinin.
source: We found that a large majority (94%) of GCaMP+ cells in GP4.3 did not show strong immunoreactivity for either marker (CR++: 2.2%; PV++: 2.9%; PV++CR++: 0.9%), whereas in the Gad2;Ai96 line a larger fraction of GCaMP+ cells were positive for CR or PV (CR++: 17%; PV++: 22%; PV++CR++: 7%; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Gad2;Ai96 mice, a larger fraction of GCaMP+ cells were positive for calretinin or parvalbumin (CR++: 17%; PV++: 22%; PV++CR++: 7%).
source: We found that a large majority (94%) of GCaMP+ cells in GP4.3 did not show strong immunoreactivity for either marker (CR++: 2.2%; PV++: 2.9%; PV++CR++: 0.9%), whereas in the Gad2;Ai96 line a larger fraction of GCaMP+ cells were positive for CR or PV (CR++: 17%; PV++: 22%; PV++CR++: 7%; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GCaMP was expressed in 38% of CR++ cells and 70% of PV++ cells in the IC of Gad2;Ai96 mice.
source: On the other hand, GCaMP was expressed in 38% of CR++ cells and 70% of PV++ cells in the IC of Gad2;Ai96 mice, while a lower fraction of CR++ (9.1%) and PV++ (13.4%) cells were positive for GCaMP in GP4.3 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A lower fraction of CR++ (9.1%) and PV++ (13.4%) cells were positive for GCaMP in GP4.3 mice.
source: On the other hand, GCaMP was expressed in 38% of CR++ cells and 70% of PV++ cells in the IC of Gad2;Ai96 mice, while a lower fraction of CR++ (9.1%) and PV++ (13.4%) cells were positive for GCaMP in GP4.3 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both increases and decreases in FGCaMP were observed during the presentation of sound stimuli.
source: Importantly, we observed both increases, which were either transient or sustained, and decreases in FGCaMP during the presentation of stimuli, and some cells showed a sharp increase in FGCaMP directly after the cessation of the sound (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The different fluorescence responses were classified as excitation, inhibitory and offset.
source: The different fluorescence responses were classified as excitation, inhibitory and offset, respectively (see Materials and methods, Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the classification scheme described in the methods and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Excitatory responses were further divided into onset and sustained classes based on the kinetics of the fluorescence change.
source: The excitatory responses were further divided into onset and sustained classes based on the kinetics of the fluorescence change (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the classification scheme and kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decrease in fluorescence upon sound stimulation was likely due to sound-evoked inhibition of spontaneous firing in these cells.
source: The decrease in fluorescence upon sound stimulation was likely due to sound-evoked inhibition of spontaneous firing in these cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed fluorescence decreases and knowledge of calcium indicator properties.

claim: Inhibitory and offset responses were not reported in earlier imaging experiments performed in anesthetized mice.
source: Inhibitory and offset responses were not reported in earlier imaging experiments performed in anesthetized mice (Ito et al., 2014; Barnstedt et al., 2015); their use of shorter stimuli did not allow a distinction between onset and sustained responses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and comparison with the current study's methods.

claim: In GP4.3 mice, 64% of the cells (696 out of 1090) showed detectable fluorescence changes in response to 1 s pure tone stimuli.
source: In GP4.3 mice, 64% of the cells (696 out of 1090) cells showed detectable fluorescence changes in response to 1 s pure tone stimuli.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data.

claim: Among responsive cells in GP4.3 mice, 30% (210 cells) showed excitatory FRAs.
source: Among the responsive cells, 30% (210 cells) showed excitatory FRAs (e.g. Figure 3—figure supplement 2), with fluorescence increasing during sound presentation; while 13% (89 cells) showed offset FRAs, with fluorescence increasing after sound presentation.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Among responsive cells in GP4.3 mice, 13% (89 cells) showed offset FRAs.
source: Among the responsive cells, 30% (210 cells) showed excitatory FRAs (e.g. Figure 3—figure supplement 2), with fluorescence increasing during sound presentation; while 13% (89 cells) showed offset FRAs, with fluorescence increasing after sound presentation.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data.

claim: Among responsive cells in GP4.3 mice, 30% (207 cells) showed inhibitory FRAs.
source: Another 30% (207 cells) showed inhibitory FRAs, with fluorescence decreasing during sound.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data.

claim: The proportion of cells showing sound-evoked inhibition was clearly higher than the 2–23% reported for anesthetized C57BL/6 mice in Willott et al. (1988a).
source: The proportion of cells showing sound-evoked inhibition was clearly higher than the 2–23% reported for anesthetized C57BL/6 mice in Willott et al. (1988a).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study supported by citation.

claim: In Gad2;Ai96 mice, 73% (247 out of 342 cells) of GCaMP6s-positive IC neurons showed consistent fluorescence responses to 1 s pure tone stimuli.
source: In Gad2;Ai96 mice 73% (247 out of 342 cells) of GCaMP6s-positive IC neurons showed consistent fluorescence responses to 1 s pure tone stimuli.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data.

claim: Among responsive cells in Gad2;Ai96 mice, 46% (115 cells) showed excitatory FRAs.
source: Among the responsive cells, 46% (115 cells) showed excitatory FRAs.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data.

claim: Among responsive cells in Gad2;Ai96 mice, 4% (11 cells) showed offset FRAs.
source: Four percent (11 cells) showed offset FRAs.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data.

claim: Among responsive cells in Gad2;Ai96 mice, 26% (65 cells) showed inhibitory FRAs.
source: Another 26% (65 cells) showed inhibitory FRAs.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data.

claim: GABAergic cells had a larger soma size than non-GABAergic cells.
source: GABAergic cells had a larger soma size, as reported previously (cat: Oliver et al., 1994; rat: Merchán et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The estimated diameters for Gad2;Ai96 and GP4.3 cells were 21.9 ± 4.9 µm and 15.9 ± 2.6 µm, respectively.
source: The estimated diameters for Gad2;Ai96 and GP4.3 cells, defined as 4/π times the square root of the ROI area in imaging experiments, were 21.9 ± 4.9 µm (mean ±s.d.) and 15.9 ± 2.6 µm, respectively (Figure 4C, p<0.001 Wilcoxon Rank Test).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Within each genotype, soma size did not differ significantly among cells with different FRA classes in GP4.3 mice.
source: Within each genotype, soma size did not differ significantly among cells with different FRA classes. For GP4.3: onset cells 12.3 ± 2.6 µm, sustained 12.5 ± 2.0 µm, inhibited 13.0 ± 1.8 µm, offset 12.3 ± 2.0 µm (p=0.112, Kruskal-Wallis Rank test).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the imaging data with statistical analysis.

claim: Onset fluorescence responses corresponded to cells whose firing rate quickly adapted during one-second long stimuli.
source: For fluorescence responses that we classified as onset, electrophysiological recordings showed that this class can represent a cell whose firing rate quickly adapted during our one-second long stimuli (example in Figure 5A–C,D left).
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous juxtacellular recording and imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sustained fluorescence responses corresponded to sustained firing.
source: We observed sustained fluorescence responses that corresponded to sustained firing (Figure 5D middle) with different amount of adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous juxtacellular recording and imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Inhibitory responses corresponded to cells that reduced their spontaneous firing upon sound stimulation.
source: Inhibitory responses corresponded to cells that reduced their spontaneous firing upon sound stimulation (Figure 5D right).
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous juxtacellular recording and imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: An action potential led to a median increase of 0.35 (GP4.3) or 0.14 (Gad2;Ai96) times the minimal fluorescence (F0).
source: We found that on average, an action potential led to a median increase of 0.35 (GP4.3; n = 5 cells) or 0.14 (Gad2;Ai96; n = 12 cells) times the minimal fluorescence (F0), with a median zero-to-peak rise time of 480 ms (GP4.3) or 560 ms (Gad2;Ai96) and a median decay time constant of 1.04 s (GP4.3) or 1.36 s (Gad2;Ai96).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the model fitting to simultaneous recording and imaging data.

claim: The model could explain between 50% and 95% of the variance in the fluorescence (median: 79%).
source: The model could explain between 50% and 95% of the variance in the fluorescence (median: 79%; average ±s.d.: 77 ± 13%).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the model fitting results.

claim: A tonotopic gradient was observed that ran along a gradient from caudolateral to rostromedial.
source: Following pooling of the data from several experiments, we observed a tonotopic gradient that ran along a gradient from caudolateral to rostromedial.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial analysis of characteristic frequencies shown in Figure 6.

claim: The tonotopic gradient reversed at the site where the CFs were the lowest.
source: The gradient reversed at the site where the CFs were the lowest.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial analysis of characteristic frequencies shown in Figure 6.

claim: The tonotopic reversal is in line with the banding patterns observed with epifluorescent calcium imaging in unanesthetized mice before and at hearing onset.
source: This reversal is in line with the banding patterns observed with epifluorescent calcium imaging in unanesthetized mice before and at hearing onset; the pre-hearing spontaneous neural activities originate from the cochlea, thus regions activated synchronously likely receive input from the same tonotopic area (Babola et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a previous study cited.

claim: The four response types showed a similar tonotopic organization.
source: The four response types showed a similar tonotopic organization, but considerable microheterogeneity.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The microheterogeneity in tonotopic organization was similar for GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons.
source: The microheterogeneity was similar for GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 165 cells (out of 1359) showed a positive correlation (r > 0.25) with facial movements during the spontaneous recording period.
source: We found that the onset of many of these spontaneous transients coincided with movement events of the animal (paw and facial movements in Figure 8A). By correlating movement and fluorescence, we detected 165 (out of 1359) cells that showed a positive correlation (r > 0.25) with facial movements during the spontaneous recording period.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the movement correlation analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: 41 cells showed spontaneous calcium transients that correlated with animal movement and could not be explained by their FRA.
source: In the end, 41 cells showed spontaneous calcium transients that correlated with animal movement and that could not be explained by their FRA, which was either inhibited-type or showed no clear pure tone evoked responses (example FRAs in Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the movement-related cells after applying exclusion criteria, shown in Figure 8.

claim: Movement-sensitive cells seemed to be enriched at the caudolateral side of the dorsal IC.
source: These cells seemed to be enriched at the caudolateral side of the dorsal IC (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the spatial distribution of movement-related cells shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: Four of the 41 movement-related cells were found in the Gad2;Ai96 line, making them 1% of GABAergic cells.
source: Four of the 41 cells were found in the Gad2;Ai96 line, in agreement with a recent report that inputs from motor or somatosensory cortex can directly target GABAergic cells (Olthof et al., 2019), and the remainder in the GP4.3 line, making them 1% of GABAergic and 4% of investigated glutamatergic cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the movement-related cells by genotype.

claim: The remainder of movement-related cells were in the GP4.3 line, making them 4% of investigated glutamatergic cells.
source: Four of the 41 cells were found in the Gad2;Ai96 line, in agreement with a recent report that inputs from motor or somatosensory cortex can directly target GABAergic cells (Olthof et al., 2019), and the remainder in the GP4.3 line, making them 1% of GABAergic and 4% of investigated glutamatergic cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the movement-related cells by genotype.

claim: The minimum frequency line aligns with the demarcation from the Allen Reference Atlas.
source: The minimum frequency line aligns with the demarcation from the Allen Reference Atlas, while that by Paxinos and Franklin lays in the orthogonal direction.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 9A and E.

claim: Modules with dense GAD67 staining were observed both medially and laterally from each of the three demarcations.
source: Modules with dense GAD67 staining, considered to be a hallmark for the LCIC, were observed both medially and laterally from each of the three demarcations (arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by the histological data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Two motion-sensitive neurons retrieved in histology both possessed dendrites that extended into a GAD67-dense module.
source: Figure 9D2 and F show two motion-sensitive neurons retrieved in histology (cells 3 and 4, marked by arrows), both of which resided in close proximity to a GAD67-dense module. We observed that although the somata of both cells seemed to reside in the extramodular regions, both possessed dendrites that extended into a GAD67-dense module (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by the histological data shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: The laterocaudal area with high frequencies is the dorsal edge of the LCIC.
source: Our findings suggest that the laterocaudal area with high frequencies is the dorsal edge of the LCIC, whereas the mediorostral part of the dorsal IC belongs to the DCIC.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the tonotopic organization and movement-related activity data.

claim: The mediorostral part of the dorsal IC belongs to the DCIC.
source: Our findings suggest that the laterocaudal area with high frequencies is the dorsal edge of the LCIC, whereas the mediorostral part of the dorsal IC belongs to the DCIC.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the tonotopic organization and movement-related activity data.

claim: The tonotopic reversal provides a functional demarcation between the dorsal and lateral cortices of the IC.
source: The tonotopic reversal would thus provide a functional demarcation between the dorsal and lateral cortices of the IC.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the tonotopic organization data.

claim: The central strip with neurons tuned to low frequencies in between the LCIC and the DCIC may be the most dorsal extension of the dorsolateral low frequency area of the CNIC.
source: The central strip with neurons tuned to low frequencies in between the LCIC and the DCIC may be the most dorsal extension of the dorsolateral low frequency area of the CNIC (Stiebler and Ehret, 1985; Barnstedt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the tonotopic organization data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The three main areas of the IC, LCIC, CNIC, DCIC, are readily accessible at the dorsal IC.
source: From our data it thus appears that the three main areas of the IC, LCIC, CNIC, DCIC, are readily accessible at the dorsal IC.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the functional organization data.
